name: Mnemic neglect
statement: People recall feedback that threatens a central part of their self-image worse than they recall the same feedback ascribed to somebody else.
meaning: The effect is a gap between two groups reading identical sentences. Participants take a bogus personality test and then read behaviours the test supposedly predicts. Half are told the behaviours describe them. Half are told they describe a stranger called Chris. The behaviours vary on two things: whether they are positive or negative, and whether the trait behind them is central to how a person sees themselves or peripheral. Recall drops in one cell only, negative behaviours on a central trait ascribed to the self. Sedikides, Green, Saunders, Skowronski and Zengel define the effect as inferior recall for self-threatening feedback compared with other kinds of feedback. Their model treats it as self-protection working at encoding: threatening feedback is processed shallowly and kept apart from stored self-knowledge, so a later memory search has few cues to find it by. That account predicts the effect should be specific to free recall, and it is. The same participants pick the same sentences out of a recognition test accurately, so the material is in memory.

origin.who: Constantine Sedikides and Jeffrey D. Green
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, volume 79, issue 6, pages 906-922
origin.note: The paper is titled 'On the self-protective nature of inconsistency-negativity management: Using the person memory paradigm to examine self-referent memory'. Its full text was not obtained, and everything said here about its four experiments is read off the authors' 2016 review. The phrase 'mnemic neglect' is not in that title. The earliest title carrying it that this search found at Crossref is Green, Pinter and Sedikides in 2005.

evidence: The founding experiment set the shape of everything after it. Participants answered 45 computer-administered items of the Michigan Omnibus Personality Inventory, an instrument invented for the study, and watched a progress display calculate their profile. They then read 32 feedback behaviours at their own pace, did a 2.5 minute filler task on geographical knowledge, and met a surprise recall task lasting about five minutes. Two judges coded the recalled items to a gist criterion and agreed on 98%. Intrusions ran at 5% across conditions and were removed. In the self condition the proportion recalled was 0.39 for positive central behaviours and 0.31 for negative central ones. In the Chris condition the same sentences gave 0.36 and 0.40. Peripheral behaviours produced no such gap, 0.18 and 0.14 for the self against 0.17 and 0.15 for Chris. Averaged unweighted across the experiments reviewed by Sedikides and Green in 2009, in a table the 2016 review takes from Wells, the pattern repeats: self 0.42 positive central and 0.30 negative central, Chris 0.40 and 0.41. The recognition result is the load-bearing one for the model. Green, Sedikides and Gregg gave participants the 32 old behaviours mixed with 32 pretested lures and found discrimination accuracy near uniform across conditions, with no penalty for the threatening items. An ego-deflation manipulation that enlarged the recall gap in the same experiment left recognition untouched. Zengel, Wells and Skowronski ran four studies on when the effect appears. It survived a delay before recall and could not be put down to how long participants looked at each behaviour. It did not emerge under cognitive load, and it waned when participants were occupied during encoding.

replication.headline: The effect holds, and it holds outside the group that named it. A meta-analysis of 93 samples by three authors with no overlap with that group puts it at g = 0.365, and Leonard Newman's laboratory has produced it four times without Sedikides or Green.
replication.detail: Liu, Deng and Yang pooled 18 studies and 93 independent samples, N = 4,989, and report g = 0.365, 95% CI 0.253 to 0.476, Z = 6.416, p < 0.001. Their abstract says most studies support the phenomenon while some find people attend to self-relevant negative information more rather than less. That figure also appears in this atlas under selective amnesia, which is where the review's subtitle sends readers who look the phrase up. The concentration question is the one worth asking, because the programme ran for over a decade inside one collaboration. It has been answered. Newman's laboratory at Syracuse has run the paradigm without either originator on the authorship. In 2009, with Nibert and Winer, it reproduced the effect among participants low in defensive pessimism, total recall of negative central behaviours 1.67 for the self against 3.08 for Chris, and not among those high in defensive pessimism, 1.75 against 1.81. Those two pairs of means are quoted here through the 2016 review, which is the only account of that paper obtained. In 2017, with Eccleston and Oikawa, it found greater mnemic neglect among Black students on a predominantly White campus than among other students, and reduced it by priming egalitarianism. In 2025, with Tan, Zhang, Ni and Fang, it found the effect in both American and Chinese participants and no sign it was larger in the American group. In 2014, with Sapolsky, Tang and Bakina, it reported four experiments showing the result depends on how long the recall period runs and on how recalled behaviours are written down. Mainz, Britz, Forster, Drüke and Gauggel tested 75 healthy men at Aachen under anodal, cathodal or sham stimulation of the medial prefrontal cortex. All three groups showed the expected effect, which the stimulation did not shift, though they used self-descriptiveness judgements of 80 trait adjectives rather than the Chris procedure.

study.cite: Liu, W., Deng, L., & Yang, H. (2025). Embracing strengths and avoiding weaknesses: a meta-analysis of the mnemic neglect effect. Memory, 33(2), 278-294.

limits: The effect is easy to remove. It goes when memory is probed by recognition instead of recall, when participants are under cognitive load at encoding, and when self-threat is defused by self-affirmation, all reported in the 2016 review. Saunders found it reversed in dysphoria, with high-dysphoric participants recalling self-threatening feedback better than low-dysphoric ones, and Zengel and colleagues report two subsidiary analyses that did not reproduce that reversal. Zengel, Skowronski, Valentiner and Sedikides report a loss of the effect among socially anxious individuals. Newman, Sapolsky, Tang and Bakina found it sensitive to the recall procedure itself, which makes the length and format of the recall task a design choice with a result attached. On what was not obtained: the Liu, Deng and Yang meta-analysis was read in abstract only at PubMed and Semantic Scholar, so nothing is said here about which 18 studies it pooled, how it handled publication bias, or how heterogeneous the samples were. Sedikides and Green's 2000 paper was not obtained and no sample size for its experiments is quoted. Hogrefe returned 403 for Newman, Sapolsky, Tang and Bakina, Brill returned 403 for Tan and colleagues, Springer required a login for Liu and Yang's 2023 study of middle-school students, and Taylor and Francis returned 403 for the meta-analysis. Green, Sedikides and Gregg's recognition paper was not obtained and is described through the review. The search covered Europe PMC by phrase, Crossref by bibliographic query, Semantic Scholar, PubMed and general web search, in English only. No preregistered direct replication of the Sedikides and Green procedure was found in any of those.
misreadings: The commonest error is the one the review's own subtitle invites. 'Selective amnesia of one's faults' reads as a claim about life, and the measurement is a recall gap of a few behaviours, minutes after reading sentences generated by a fake personality test. Nothing here concerns autobiographical memory or forgetting real events. The second error is to read it as ordinary negativity bias. The comparison is against the identical sentences ascribed to Chris, and against peripheral traits, both of which recall fine. What the effect tracks is threat, not unpleasantness. The third is to treat the forgetting as loss. Recognition is intact, so the sentences are stored and the failure is at retrieval, which is why the model talks about encoding depth and cue linkage rather than erasure. The fourth is to take g = 0.365 as a general property of self-relevant memory. It is an average across conditions that include ones where the effect vanishes and one clinical group where it turns around. A reader should also not assume the literature is one laboratory talking to itself. It began that way and has not stayed that way.

sources.text: Sedikides, C., Green, J. D., Saunders, J., Skowronski, J. J., & Zengel, B. (2016). Mnemic neglect: Selective amnesia of one's faults. European Review of Social Psychology, 27(1), 1-62. Accepted manuscript at the Strathclyde repository, converted to text and re-extracted a second time to confirm every figure quoted. The source for the definition, the paradigm, Table 1a and Table 1b, the recognition results, and the descriptions of Newman et al. 2009 and 2014.

Sedikides, C., & Green, J. D. (2000). On the self-protective nature of inconsistency-negativity management: Using the person memory paradigm to examine self-referent memory. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(6), 906-922. Crossref and PubMed records only; not obtained. The founding paper.

Liu, W., Deng, L., & Yang, H. (2025). Embracing strengths and avoiding weaknesses: a meta-analysis of the mnemic neglect effect. Memory, 33(2), 278-294. Abstract read at PubMed and again at Semantic Scholar; full text behind a 403 at Taylor and Francis. The source for g = 0.365 and its interval.

Newman, L. S., Nibert, J. A., & Winer, E. S. (2009). Mnemic neglect is not an artifact of expectancy: The moderating role of defensive pessimism. European Journal of Social Psychology, 39(3), 477-486. Crossref record only; not obtained. Its means are quoted here through the 2016 review.

Newman, L. S., Sapolsky, M. S., Tang, Y., & Bakina, D. A. (2014). What's recalled depends on the nature of the recall procedure: The case of mnemic neglect. Social Psychology, 45(2), 93-102. Crossref record and the Unpaywall entry giving all four authors' affiliation as Syracuse University; Hogrefe returned 403. Its findings are described through the 2016 review.

Newman, L. S., Eccleston, C. P., & Oikawa, M. (2017). Ignoring biased feedback: Membership in a stigmatized group as a moderator of mnemic neglect. The Journal of Social Psychology, 157(2), 152-164. Abstract read at Europe PMC and verified at PubMed; full text not obtained.

Tan, M., Newman, L. S., Zhang, B., Ni, J., & Fang, J. (2025). Mnemic Neglect in the United States and China: a Cross-cultural Investigation of Spontaneous Self-protection. Journal of Cognition and Culture, 26(1-2), 5-29. Abstract read at Crossref and again at Semantic Scholar; Brill returned 403 for the full text.

Zengel, B., Wells, B. M., & Skowronski, J. J. (2018). The waxing and waning of mnemic neglect. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 114(5), 719-734. Abstract read at Europe PMC and verified at PubMed; the source for the four studies on delay, looking time and cognitive load.

Mainz, V., Britz, S., Forster, S. D., Drüke, B., & Gauggel, S. (2020). Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation of the Medial Prefrontal Cortex Has No Specific Effect on Self-referential Processes. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 14, 56. Abstract read at Europe PMC and verified at PubMed; the source for the 75 participants and for all three stimulation groups showing the effect.

Green, J. D., Sedikides, C., & Gregg, A. P. (2008). Forgotten but not gone: The recall and recognition of self-threatening memories. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 44(3), 547-561. Crossref record only; not obtained. The recognition findings are described through the 2016 review.

Saunders, J. (2011). Reversed mnemic neglect of self-threatening memories in dysphoria. Cognition and Emotion, 25(5), 854-867. Crossref record only; not obtained. Described through the 2016 review, which also reports the two subsidiary non-replications of the reversal.

Zengel, B., Skowronski, J. J., Valentiner, D. P., & Sedikides, C. (2015). Loss of Mnemic Neglect Among Socially Anxious Individuals. Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 34(4), 322-347. Crossref record and title only; not obtained.

Liu, W., & Yang, H. (2023). The mnemic neglect effect in middle school students: a study based on two fundamental dimensions of social cognition. Current Psychology, 43(18), 16094-16103. Crossref record only; Springer required a login. Cited as evidence that the paradigm is being run outside the originating group, not for its contents.
